FEHA ADMINISTRATIVE COMPLAINT WITH CALIFORNIA'S CIVIL RIGHTS DEPARTMENT — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Lee · Acme Corp.

INFORMATION AND BACKGROUND — FEHA ADMINISTRATIVE COMPLAINT
I, Jordan Lee, am completing this information sheet in connection with a possible administrative complaint against Acme Corp. under California's Fair Employment and Housing Act (FEHA), filed with California's Civil Rights Department (CRD). The practice I believe may have been unlawful is described here as: Terminated shortly after requesting a religious accommodation. The date on which I believe the alleged unlawful practice occurred is stated here as March 14, 2026. If a complaint has already been filed with the Civil Rights Department, the date it was filed is stated here as April 1, 2026; if a right-to-sue notice has already been issued, the date of that notice is stated here as May 15, 2026. This information sheet describes, using the statutes' own text, how the CRD administrative complaint process works — the filing deadline, what a complaint must contain, how CRD's investigation process relates to the option of requesting an immediate right-to-sue notice, and the legal effect and filing deadline that follow once a right-to-sue notice issues. It is not a CRD intake form, not a verified complaint, not a right-to-sue notice, not a court filing, and not a legal determination of any kind. Completing this information sheet does not file a complaint with the Civil Rights Department, does not request or obtain a right-to-sue notice, and does not determine that any specific practice by Acme Corp. was unlawful, that any specific complaint would be timely, or that any specific claim is valid. Only the Civil Rights Department, a court, or another body with legal authority to decide the question can make those determinations.

THE THREE-YEAR DEADLINE TO FILE A FEHA COMPLAINT WITH THE CIVIL RIGHTS DEPARTMENT
California law sets a specific deadline for filing an administrative complaint alleging a FEHA employment-discrimination, harassment, or retaliation violation with the Civil Rights Department: three years from the date the alleged unlawful practice occurred. This three-year period applies to complaints alleging a violation of the FEHA employment-practices article (the article beginning with Government Code section 12940) — the article that contains FEHA's core discrimination, harassment, and retaliation prohibitions. The statute sets other, different deadlines for complaints alleging violations of certain other, non-FEHA-employment statutes administered by the same department, which this clause does not address.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "A complaint alleging a violation of Section 51.9 of the Civil Code or any other violation of Article 1 (commencing with Section 12940) of Chapter 6 shall not be filed after the expiration of three years from the date upon which the unlawful practice or refusal to cooperate occurred."
  — Cal. Gov't Code § 12960(e)(5) (California Legislative Information text), California Government Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=12960.)
  Known gap: This clause quotes a single subdivision, Government Code section 12960(e)(5), current as most recently amended by Stats. 2025, Ch. 321 (SB 477), effective January 1, 2026. The same subdivision (e) of section 12960 also sets different filing deadlines for complaints alleging violations of several other statutes (Civil Code sections 51, 51.5, 51.7, 51.9, 52.5, 54, 54.1, and 54.2, Labor Code section 1197.5, and the state's own nondiscrimination-in-programs statute) — this clause does not restate those other deadlines, which are not FEHA employment claims. Section 12960(e)(6), also not quoted here, lists several categories of extension to the filing periods (a 90-day discovery-based extension, an extension tied to correcting a misidentified employer, an extension tied to discovering a defendant's identity in a Civil Code section 51.7 case, and an extension tied to reaching the age of majority) — this document does not address whether any such extension applies to a specific complaint. Section 12960(f), also not quoted here, separately tolls the time to file a civil action (as distinct from the time to file the administrative complaint itself) while an administrative complaint remains pending with the department, and states that this tolling applies retroactively but does not revive an already-lapsed claim; this document does not address civil-action-deadline tolling for claims other than the one-year deadline following a right-to-sue notice, addressed in a separate clause of this document. This document does not determine whether any specific complaint was, or would be, filed within the applicable deadline, or whether any extension or tolling provision applies to any specific set of facts.

HOW A FEHA COMPLAINT IS FILED AND WHAT IT MUST CONTAIN
Under the statute governing this process, filing a complaint with the Civil Rights Department means filing an intake form with the department; the operative filing date of the resulting verified complaint relates back to the date the intake form was filed. Any person claiming to be aggrieved by an alleged unlawful practice may file with the department a verified complaint, in writing, that states the name and address of the person, employer, labor organization, or employment agency alleged to have committed the unlawful practice, sets forth the particulars of the alleged practice, and contains any other information the department may require. The department's own director, or the director's authorized representative, may separately make, sign, and file a complaint on that person's behalf.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "For purposes of this section, filing a complaint means filing an intake form with the department and the operative date of the verified complaint relates back to the filing of the intake form."
  — Cal. Gov't Code § 12960(b) (California Legislative Information text), California Government Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=12960.)
  "Any person claiming to be aggrieved by an alleged unlawful practice may file with the department a verified complaint, in writing, that shall state the name and address of the person, employer, labor organization, or employment agency alleged to have committed the unlawful practice complained of, and that shall set forth the particulars thereof and contain other information as may be required by the department."
  — Cal. Gov't Code § 12960(c) (California Legislative Information text), California Government Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=12960.)
  Known gap: This clause combines two citations that are subdivisions of the same statutory section, Government Code section 12960(b) and section 12960(c), rather than two independent sources -- disclosed here explicitly. This document does not describe the department's current online intake form itself, its specific fields, or any non-statutory administrative filing procedure the department may use to implement this statutory framework; it states what the statute itself requires and permits. This document does not determine that a specific written submission satisfies the verified-complaint requirement, or that a specific intake filing date has been correctly established.

THE CIVIL RIGHTS DEPARTMENT'S INVESTIGATION, CONCILIATION, AND MANDATORY DISPUTE RESOLUTION
Once a complaint is filed, the statute contemplates that the Civil Rights Department will first attempt to eliminate an alleged unlawful practice through conference, conciliation, mediation, or persuasion; only if that effort fails -- or, in the director's discretion, in advance of it if circumstances warrant -- may the department's director bring a civil action in the department's own name, acting in the public interest, on behalf of the person claiming to be aggrieved. Before the department may file that kind of civil action, the statute separately requires all parties to participate in mandatory dispute resolution within the department's own internal dispute resolution division, free of charge to the parties, in an effort to resolve the dispute without litigation.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "In the case of failure to eliminate an unlawful practice under this part through conference, conciliation, mediation, or persuasion, or in advance thereof if circumstances warrant, the director in the director’s discretion may bring a civil action in the name of the department, acting in the public interest, on behalf of the person claiming to be aggrieved."
  — Cal. Gov't Code § 12965(a)(1) (California Legislative Information text), California Government Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=12965.)
  "Prior to filing a civil action, the department shall require all parties to participate in mandatory dispute resolution in the department’s internal dispute resolution division free of charge to the parties in an effort to resolve the dispute without litigation."
  — Cal. Gov't Code § 12965(a)(2) (California Legislative Information text), California Government Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=12965.)
  Known gap: This clause combines two citations that are subdivisions of the same statutory section, Government Code section 12965(a)(1) and section 12965(a)(2), rather than two independent sources -- disclosed here explicitly. This clause describes only the department-initiated civil-action pathway and the mandatory dispute-resolution step that precedes it; it does not describe the department's internal investigative methods or timeline in the detail the department's own regulations may provide, and it does not describe the separate right of the person claiming to be aggrieved to request a right-to-sue notice instead of waiting on this process, which is addressed in a separate clause of this document. This document does not determine whether the department will investigate, conciliate, or bring a civil action on any specific complaint, or how long any specific investigation will take.

REQUESTING A RIGHT-TO-SUE NOTICE INSTEAD OF WAITING FOR THE DEPARTMENT TO ACT
The statute gives the person claiming to be aggrieved an alternative to waiting for the department's own investigation or civil action to run its course. If a civil action is not brought by the department within 150 days after the complaint is filed, or if the department earlier determines that no civil action will be brought, the statute requires the department to notify that person in writing that the department will issue a right-to-sue notice on request. If the person does not request a right-to-sue notice, the department instead issues it upon completing its investigation, and no later than one year after the complaint was filed.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "if a civil action is not brought by the department pursuant to subdivision (a) within 150 days after the filing of a complaint, or if the department earlier determines that no civil action will be brought pursuant to subdivision (a), the department shall promptly notify, in writing, the person claiming to be aggrieved that the department shall issue, on request, the right-to-sue notice."
  — Cal. Gov't Code § 12965(c)(1)(A) (California Legislative Information text), California Government Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=12965.)
  Known gap: This clause quotes a single statutory subdivision, Government Code section 12965(c)(1)(A). This document uses the phrase "immediate right-to-sue" as this project's own description of the practical effect of requesting a right-to-sue notice on request rather than waiting for the department's investigation to complete; that exact phrase does not appear in the quoted statutory text itself, and this document does not describe the department's current online or administrative procedure for making that request, which may differ in detail from what the statute itself states. This document does not determine whether requesting an immediate right-to-sue notice, or instead allowing the department's investigation to proceed, would be more advantageous in any specific case, and does not itself request a right-to-sue notice or file anything with the department.

THE RIGHT-TO-SUE NOTICE'S LEGAL EFFECT AND THE ONE-YEAR DEADLINE TO SUE
A right-to-sue notice issued under this statute must indicate that the person claiming to be aggrieved may bring a civil action against the person, employer, labor organization, or employment agency named in the verified complaint -- and that the civil action must be brought within one year from the date of that notice. The statute gives California's superior courts jurisdiction over these civil actions, and states that the aggrieved person may file directly in those courts.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "The notices specified in subparagraphs (A), (B), and (C) shall indicate that the person claiming to be aggrieved may bring a civil action under this part against the person, employer, labor organization, or employment agency named in the verified complaint within one year from the date of that notice."
  — Cal. Gov't Code § 12965(c)(1)(D) (California Legislative Information text), California Government Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=12965.)
  "The superior courts of the State of California shall have jurisdiction of actions brought pursuant to this section, and the aggrieved person may file in these courts."
  — Cal. Gov't Code § 12965(c)(3) (California Legislative Information text), California Government Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=12965.)
  Known gap: This clause combines two citations that are subdivisions of the same statutory section but different subdivisions -- Government Code section 12965(c)(1)(D) and section 12965(c)(3) -- disclosed here explicitly rather than presented as independent sources. Section 12965(c)(1)(E), not separately quoted here, states that this one-year notice-and-deadline paragraph applies only to complaints alleging unlawful employment practices under the FEHA employment-practices article (the article beginning with Government Code section 12940) -- the category of claim this document addresses. Section 12965(c)(1)(F), and separately section 12965(e) and (f), each not quoted here, set out specific tolling rules that can extend this one-year deadline (including tolling during the department's own dispute-resolution proceedings, tolling under a written agreement between the department and a respondent, and tolling tied to a concurrently filed federal EEOC charge that the department defers) -- this document does not determine whether any such tolling rule applies to any specific right-to-sue notice or claim. This document does not itself constitute a right-to-sue notice, does not determine that any right-to-sue notice has actually issued in any specific case, and does not calculate or confirm any specific one-year deadline.

CLOSING AND SIGNATURE BLOCK — FEHA ADMINISTRATIVE COMPLAINT INFORMATION SHEET
I declare that the information above is true and correct to the best of my knowledge.

Executed on September 4, 2026 at Sacramento, California.
